1:
Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter in its place: three prophecies form a trilogy, the first treating Ethiopia in language of the sublimest pathos, this one treating Egypt in a calmer descriptive tone, and the third handling both in the style of historic prose—one kingdom throughout, but seen first as the ruling nation, then as the conquered, then as a whole. They add the reason for the attention paid to Egypt, that no nation on earth was so mixed up with the history of the kingdom of God, and that Israel was charged never to forget having been sheltered there. Charles Ellicott makes the same point about the conquered nation being distinguished from its conqueror, and hears in the opening words a long-delayed judgment arriving swift as a cloud driven by the storm-wind. Adam Clarke supplies the history the chapter is thought to fit: after the destruction of the Assyrian army the affairs of Egypt fell into intestine broils and then perfect anarchy, followed by a tyranny of twelve princes who divided the country between them, then the fifty-four years of a single ruler, then conquest by the Babylonians and after them the Persians, whose yoke was so grievous that the coming of the Greeks might well be reckoned a deliverance.

Matthew Henry and John Calvin both explain why the prophecy was needed by Judah rather than Egypt. Henry observes that among the unbelieving Jews there remained much of the humour of the fathers who wished for a captain to take them back, and that while the alliance held they stood in no awe of God’s judgments—so Egypt had to be mortified. Calvin says the same and adds the double harm: the confidence puffed them up, and whenever God chastised them they sheltered behind Egyptian power as though human resources could make his judgments void. Henry then reads the opening image as a state entrance, a judge going to the bench or a general taking the field, and notes what the chapter never mentions—a foreign invader—since God raises the causes of destruction from within. John Wesley hears in the swift cloud that the judgment will come speedily, unexpectedly and unavoidably. On the idols, Henry says idolatry had rooted deeper in Egypt than in any land besides, and Calvin lists what they worshipped, cats and oxen and crocodiles and even onions and plants of every sort; but Calvin also dismisses a favourite application, the notion that the verse was fulfilled when the idols fell at the coming of the infant Christ, which he says the passage has been perverted to prove and which does not deserve refutation.

The civil war of the second verse is where history and theology meet. John Gill notes that the ruin comes by internal quarrels and not by any foreign invasion. Ellicott traces the discord to a political cause, the overthrow of the Ethiopian power by the Assyrian king, after which the district chiefs who had owned that suzerainty would naturally assert independence—and cites a Greek historian for the breaking up of Egypt into a rule of twelve. Wesley reports the same twelve kingdoms and their many cruel wars. Keil and Delitzsch describe the inward collapse, a people once shrewd now at their wits’ end, the spirit poured out so that nothing is left of intelligence or resolution. Calvin refuses to let the political cause stand alone: nations never rise in sedition unless God sets them against one another, as a man brings gladiators out to the combat, so that as friendship among citizens is evidence of his favour, mutual rage is evidence of his vengeance. He notes that the prophet advances by degrees to what is more monstrous still, kinsmen taking arms against each other—for if men are worse than beasts in forgetting their common nature, brethren fighting is worse yet—and explains the last term as the districts into which Egypt was divided.
3:
John Gill is careful which faculty fails: not the courage, taken away in the verse before, but wisdom and understanding—and he recalls what that means for Egypt, the mother and mistress of the liberal arts, where philosophers travelled to learn, so that what had been a river full of water was now to be drained dry. John Calvin presses the irony harder. The Egyptians thought themselves so far above other nations that they called them all barbarians, claiming to have invented learning and to be the workshop of every art; had this prediction reached them they would have laughed, thinking the waters of the sea would dry up sooner than their prudence fail. Charles Ellicott takes the diviners historically: the old reputation of Egypt for magic seems to have continued, the mutterers probably distinguished by some form of ventriloquism, and a season of panic, when statesmen have nothing to advise, was as sure to breed oracles there as at Athens in its own perils. Adam Clarke gives only an old English rendering of the four classes named.

The cruel lord is identified variously. Gill rejects the two commonest readings, the Assyrian invader and the Babylonian, and offers either the twelve tyrants—since the noun is plural although the adjective is singular—or the one who conquered the other eleven and ruled fifty-four years with great rigour. John Wesley names the same man. Clarke reads the plural too but fills it differently, with the Babylonian first and then the whole succession of Persian kings, and notes a manuscript and three versions supporting it. Ellicott declines to choose, observing that the later history of Egypt offers so many pictures of oppressive government that five different rulers have each in turn been identified with this one. Calvin is interested less in the name than in the grammar and its weight: the plural is harder to bear than a single master, and the power of such a ruler too great for an easy recovery of liberty—to keep what has been won being often harder than to win it. He allows an alternative, that the princes of small nations deal more gently than great monarchs, who, reckoning their power unlimited, set no bounds to what they do.

The drying of the river is where the chapter’s geography matters. Keil and Delitzsch mark a fresh misfortune, the Nile drying and the fertility of the land disappearing with it, and render the sequel with the arms of the river spreading a stench, the channels parched, reed and rush shrivelled. Ellicott identifies the sea with the Nile itself, as an ancient poet did, or possibly with one branch of it, and notes that the White and Blue Niles are in their own language the White and Blue Seas; he reads what follows as the effect partly of a failed annual rising and partly of irrigation works neglected during the anarchy already foretold. Gill reports the figurative readings—a destruction compared to a drying river, or the failure of the sea trade—but prefers the literal, adding that the Nile might itself be called a sea, so large a confluence of water. Wesley works out the mechanics: the river poured its waters into the sea by seven famous mouths, so when it failed the waters truly failed from the sea, and no forced sense of the word is needed; he adds that the drying is not total but very great. Clarke states the consequence in a sentence, that with little or no rain in the country a failed inundation must leave the land barren. Calvin takes the verse as the answer to Egyptian confidence in her defences: they reckoned themselves invincible because the sea and the river surrounded them, and historians confirm how hard entry was—much as the people of Venice in his own day supposed themselves impregnable behind deep ditches; but fortresses, he says, are useless when God has determined to punish.
6:
The turning away of the rivers is disputed in sense and reference alike. Charles Ellicott would read that the river stagnates, the inundation having failed, and takes the second noun not as brooks of defence but as a proper name, the singular of the dual form used for Egypt, standing here for the lower country as distinct from the upper, its root sense being a fortified land; the flags, he adds, are strictly the papyrus, the brooks the canals of the delta. Adam Clarke proposes that the verb means to become putrid, a sense he takes from a cognate language and thinks suits the place better than anything yet offered, noting that the form is very irregular and the grammarians give no probable account of it. John Gill reports a reading that makes the kings of Egypt the ones who turned the river, ascribing to the twelve tyrants the digging of a great lake with two pyramids in it and a labyrinth beside it—which he corrects, since only the labyrinth was theirs, the lake having been made centuries earlier by the king it was named for, and having helped the river rather than hurt it by taking its overflow and returning water when it failed. John Wesley keeps it simple: the distributing channels must go dry when the river feeding them does, and the reeds that made their boats with them.

John Calvin stops on the difficulty the passage raises. The embankments will be useless because the Nile is to be dried up—but it is certain, he says, that the Nile was not laid dry, and equally certain that the prophet did not foretell what was never accomplished. His answer is that our stupidity requires such calamities to be painted in a lively manner, set as it were before our eyes, since we need a picture that will impress the mind and rouse us to consider judgments we otherwise despise. On the following verse he takes the word for the source rather than the marshes, so the drying reaches the fountain itself, which seldom fails when torrents do—a threat with force in a country where rain seldom falls and the Nile supplies its place, so a scanty overflow means famine.

The reeds and the fishermen give room for antiquarian interests. Gill identifies the reed on the banks as the one the Greeks called papyrus, from which the words paper and book descend, and dates the making of paper from it to the prophet’s own age, many hundred years before the period some assign to its invention. Wesley describes the process, the reed divided with a needle into thin broad leaves which were dried and used for writing, and so a very good commodity. Ellicott would render the clause the meadows by the Nile, notes that the word for brooks is used specifically of that river, and reads the last verbs as drying up and vanishing, so that the valley becomes as parched as the desert on either side of it. On the fishers, Gill assembles the evidence that fish were the staple: few other living creatures were eaten, out of superstition; the priests were forbidden fish though the people were not; and a historian records the daily revenue the fishery brought the treasury, some men living on nothing but fish gutted and dried in the sun. Clarke cites the same historian for the incredible numbers of fish in the river and still more in the lakes; Ellicott notes that fish always formed part of the working man’s diet and that Egyptian pictures constantly show the two ways of taking them, by hook and by net. Calvin explains the rhetoric—prophets name whatever a country abounds in, vines for a vine-country, gold where there is gold—and prefers to say the fishers shall be weakened rather than cut off, since a nation deprived of its ordinary food must fall into great poverty.
9:
The linen trade is described precisely. Charles Ellicott notes that the fine flax served especially for the dress of the priests and the wrappings of the dead, and would render the second class not weavers of networks but makers of white cloths, the cotton or byssus fabrics Egypt was famous for. Adam Clarke takes the first term as flax dressed on the heckle or comb, and quotes an old English version. John Calvin hesitates between the two trades: weaving nets and fishing go naturally together, but if the word means very fine linens the second clause is about other work of the loom, of the most elegant kind—and he proposes that the term for the openwork means costly garments whose value rose with the delicacy of their texture, so that the prophet taunts the Egyptians with their luxury, as though they clothed themselves in a net. John Gill and John Wesley keep to the plain point, that fine linen was one of the country’s best commodities and there would be neither flax to work nor cloth to sell.

The verse that follows is the chapter’s most doubtful, and none pretends otherwise. Clarke calls the line obscure and lays out three unreconciled readings without choosing: one authority makes the first word granaries; the word he renders gain some take for nets or enclosures; and the Greek turns it into strong drink, followed by another old version, so the line becomes a lament of those who make barley wine, grieved in soul—interpretations he submits to the reader’s judgment. Gill reports that the noun means foundations and may point to the dams and banks that held the water, but prefers a sense he finds in later Hebrew, nets, so that the nets lie and rot for want of use. Ellicott abandons the fishery altogether and reads the pillars of the state broken in pieces and all who work for wages troubled in mind, citing the sense of foundations elsewhere. Calvin stays with the pools: where fish are plentiful they are kept in ponds, since otherwise the catch must be sold cheap and a cast of the net is not always successful—now it will be possible neither to take fish nor keep them, and the pools will be of no use. Wesley says only that the fish will die for want of water.

On the princes of Zoan the commentators supply the place and the posture. Gill and Ellicott agree on the city, the Tanis of the Greeks, founded within seven years of Hebron and long a royal residence, capital of the nome named after it; Gill adds that it was the scene of the ancient miracles before Pharaoh. Ellicott sketches the speakers as priest-princes and priest-magicians who boast at once of wisdom and ancestry and address their king in something like a tone of superiority, claiming to be the only counsellors—a claim the prophet challenges by asking whether they can disclose, as he can, what is coming on their country. Wesley hears the same self-importance in the boast that wisdom is hereditary and natural to them, and asks why they put such foolish words into their master’s mouth. Calvin observes the rhetorical strategy of calling men wise while accusing them of folly, which is a kind of concession, and turns the verse into an exclamation—where is that wisdom of Egypt, and where are the counsellors who held all other men in contempt, and why do they not preserve their kingdom? His moral is that God lets men achieve enough to gain a reputation, then infatuates them, so for all their sagacity they act more foolishly than children. Clarke is on the grammar: the sentence as it stands wants a verb, and where one scholar would mend it by transposing two words, Clarke thinks the Latin translator had a copy with the verb supplied, which makes the construction clear and the transposition unnecessary.
12:
John Calvin turns the challenge to the wise men into an essay on how the future can be known at all. He allows three ways: chiefly the revelation of the Spirit, which alone gives certainty and comes by the rare gift of prophecy; then astronomy; then the comparison of past events, from which ordinary prudence is got. Of the second he is guarded: the stars may suggest famine or plenty or pestilence, but nothing certain, since it rests on conjecture, and the actions of men are not governed by them, whatever idle astrologers imagine. He adds a contemporary complaint, that many such men in his own day work into the confidence of princes and people as though they knew everything present and future; princes listen and receive them as gods, and deserve to be imposed upon, being justly punished for their curiosity. The Egyptian diviners were of that kind, consulted on the smallest and greatest affairs and answered as oracles—so the prophet mocks them: how shall they tell what they do not know, and have they been admitted to the counsel of God? John Gill identifies the same class, the magicians and astrologers the king consulted and paid; Adam Clarke notes that a verb seems to have dropped out, two manuscripts adding a let them come which he thinks genuine, since without it the following conjunction is merely embarrassing.

On the second city they are more confident than the evidence allows. Charles Ellicott identifies Noph with Memphis, weighs two derivations and prefers the one meaning place of the good, and calls it a chief royal city of the lower country and seat of the ruling dynasty; John Wesley gives the same identification and its variant spelling. Calvin admits he cannot determine which cities are meant, and reports the opinion that one was Alexandria, whose antiquity he argues from Scripture against those who make Alexander its founder—the place having been often destroyed, and the king, he says, only repairing what he did not build. On the last phrase Ellicott reads the corner-stone of the castes, the word describing the superiority the priest-rulers claimed; Calvin takes it for the chief part of a building on which the whole weight rests; Wesley reads it of the chief counsellors, and notes that the prophet calls the provinces tribes by a term borrowed from his own people. Clarke adds that a great weight of manuscripts and editions drops a conjunction here, and the word for stay should be pointed as a plural, pillars.

The poured-out spirit of giddiness raises the chapter’s hardest question, and Calvin faces it. He grants that the ruin of a prudent nation by its leaders’ stupidity is incredible enough to need ascribing to God’s judgment, so no one may put it down to chance—but denies that the prophet makes God the author of the folly in any sense that leaves the Egyptians a grievance. Men have no understanding of their own, and if God withholds his Spirit we have no standing to dispute, since what he gives is free gift. He then refuses the obvious detour: it is superfluous, he says, to dispute here about predestination, since the Lord is punishing open vice, and one who acts justly in punishing cannot be called the author of sin—the punishment being executed by delivering men over to the adversary, who strictly speaking mingles the giddiness. Keil and Delitzsch put it in a line: the spirit God pours out is not only a spirit of salvation but also of judgment. Gill has the cup mingled and given them to drink, and reads the blindness as judicial, imposed for their boasting. Ellicott renders it a spirit of giddiness poured out, and draws the picture: prostrate or vacillating amid the wrecks of frustrated plans, they are as a drunkard staggering in his own foulness. Wesley completes the image: the man so drunk he reels and vomits.
15:
The paralysis is total, and the phrase for it draws a curiosity. John Gill spells out what work is left—no flax, no fish, no rushes for paper, and no power in their hands to deliver themselves—while John Calvin takes head and tail for all ranks from the highest to the lowest, or possibly for the order men keep in their actions, and draws the moral that the beginning and the end of everything depend on God, since counsel and success are both to be asked of him. Charles Ellicott agrees that the figure covers all classes. Adam Clarke reports a stranger opinion, on a rabbi’s authority, that some have supposed the words to mean the dragon’s head and tail and to be aimed at those conversant in astronomy and astrology.

The comparison to women is where Calvin is most careful. He knows the reading that takes it as an allusion to a custom for which the old historians reproached the Egyptians, that by an inversion of things women went out and transacted the affairs of state while men did the work of women; and he grants the prophet may have had it in view, but on a nearer look rejects the conjecture, since the verse threatens a judgment rather than charging a national habit—it does not say the Egyptian heart was effeminate but that dread will make it so. He adds, in fairness to them, that heathen writers relate many of their exploits and that they wished to keep the renown of warlike men, which is why the change is so striking a display of heaven’s judgment. Ellicott takes the image as common property, natural to the poetry of all countries, and quotes an epic taunt about women rather than men. Gill glosses it as weak, fearful and timorous, even in their military force; John Wesley supplies the cause, that they perceive they are not fighting with men only; and Clarke notes a plural verb in one manuscript and two versions, which he explicitly declines to propose as an emendation, since either form will do.

Why the land of Judah should terrify Egypt is answered three ways. Gill denies that war between them is meant, since they were in strict alliance, and explains the panic as the effect of hearing what the invasion had done to Judah: with only one narrow country between them the road lay open, and they might well reflect that if such judgments fell on God’s own people they could expect worse—the more so as they had helped to draw that people into idolatry. Clarke agrees on the geography, the threatening hand shaken over Egypt from the side through which the invading army would march, and glosses the noun as the kind of terror that drives a man to his wit’s end and makes him reel like a drunkard. Calvin knows the simpler reading, that Judah will be an astonishment as other lands are, but thinks the point is why God should deal so with Egypt at all—because the Egyptians had ruined the Jews by turning them from the confidence they owed to God, as princes commonly court their neighbours and offer help so as to use them afterwards. Both parties were punished, the one for listening where God had forbidden them to go, the other for the solicitation; and Calvin fixes the relation in an image, that the look of a woman brings a blush to the man who seduced her once the shame is uncovered and God appears as the avenger of the marriage bond. Keil and Delitzsch add the observation that changes the direction of the chapter: what has begun is only slavish fear, but it is the beginning of a turn to something better. Wesley reads it as the moment when Egypt apprehends that God is calling them to account for their injuries.
18:
The turn to mercy is marked by all. Matthew Henry says the sun of comfort breaks out of the threatening clouds, and the blessing is not a revived trade or a replenished river but the true religion—a grace worth more than all the natural wealth of Egypt. He knows of no event answering to it short of the conversion of Egypt to the faith of Christ and the churches that flourished there for ages. On the language of Canaan he is epigrammatic: converting grace, by changing the heart, changes the language, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. John Calvin reads the phrase as agreement in religion—the tongue standing for confession, the holy tongue commended not for its dialect but for the truth it carried—then guards it fiercely. Harmony must be sought, but not by a middle course, as those seek it who overturn religion and still wish to be thought peace-makers: away with such fickle and changeful tongues, for the Egyptians cannot speak the language of Canaan until they have given up their own.

How many the five cities are, and what the sixth is called, divides them. John Gill reports and rejects a reading that makes the whole prophecy allegorical, Egypt standing for Rome and the five cities for the kingdoms that broke away at the Reformation, and prefers a literal Egypt, with five taken for so many chief cities or an uncertain number. Calvin takes it arithmetically the other way, five out of six saved and only the sixth part destroyed. John Wesley reads the same proportion. Henry offers both: the named city may be the city of the sun, the most infamous of them for idolatry; or for every five cities embracing religion one will reject it and be called a city of destruction.

The name is the chapter’s hardest textual problem, and Adam Clarke lays it all out without deciding. The reading may have been city of the sun, which fifteen manuscripts, seven editions and four versions support; the present city of destruction may have been introduced by Palestinian Jews to register their detestation of the schismatic Egyptian temple, or be the prophet’s own change of one letter, as elsewhere a house of God is turned into a house of iniquity; another scholar argues from a cognate language that the word means a lion and identifies the place as Leontopolis; and the Greek gives city of righteousness, a name he thinks contrived by the party that wanted the temple credited. The reading being so uncertain, he concludes, no one can say what city was meant. Charles Ellicott reaches the same play on words but is confident of its purpose, that it announced the demolition of the sun-idols, and dismisses the renderings of rescue, protection and restoration as inadequately grounded. Calvin says flatly that those who read sun have mistaken one letter for another resembling it, and that Heliopolis does not suit the context. On the altar, Keil and Delitzsch identify this verse, and not the one before, as the text Onias appealed to when he sought leave to build; Gill and Henry both recount that building and refuse it as the fulfilment, Henry because the pious regarded it as an affront to Jerusalem, Gill because the altar meant is not material but Christ himself. Calvin calls the appeal a wicked and malicious perversion, and adds that the same trick is worked in his own day on a verse of Malachi to defend the mass. Ellicott, more mildly, takes the altar for one of witness rather than rival worship, and traces the influence that followed, from settlers on the frontier to the emigration to Alexandria and the Greek translation of the Scriptures. Wesley reduces it to a rule: the altar stands for worship, and nothing is commoner in the prophets than to speak of gospel worship in the phrases of the law.
20:
The promise of a saviour is taken by all as more than political. John Calvin insists on the order of grace: God must call us before we can call on him, and the crying of this verse proceeds from faith, since no one resorts there till he has been allured by God’s goodness. The saviour can be no other than Christ, since Egypt was not delivered from its distresses until his doctrine reached it—four centuries of war having wasted the country almost to ruin, and then, when one would think it finished, it is converted. He turns it on his own age: would the world learnt the lesson now, after calamities enough to bring it to the brink. Charles Ellicott reads the verse as anticipating the later teaching that worship is not tied to a place, so that prayers offered in Egypt find as immediate access as if offered in the temple, and adds that God would send a deliverer as he sent the judges to Israel—with a higher fulfilment when the gospel brought peace to the weary in Egypt as in Galilee, in Alexandria as in Jerusalem.

What kind of worship is promised divides the two closest readers. Ellicott poses it as a question: did the prophet think of slain victims and meal offerings as literally presented in Egypt, or look past the symbol to the thing symbolised? The builders of the rival temple took the first view; those who have entered into his mind, he thinks, will incline to the second—though a literal fulfilment has been found in a Greek king coming to Jerusalem to sacrifice. Calvin answers outright: what use would sacrifices be after the manifestation of Christ? The words describe confession of faith and calling on God, and under the shadow of the ceremonies we understand the reasonable worship the apostle speaks of. He fastens instead on the knowledge twice mentioned, the foundation of all religion and the key that opens the gate of the kingdom—there being no knowledge without doctrine, and so no worship God approves that is not guided by it, whatever men contrive of themselves. Ellicott marks what he calls the catholicity of the prophet’s mind, that the highest of blessings was not Israel’s exclusive inheritance but shared with the nation she had most reason to count a hereditary enemy. Gill traces the means, the Scriptures translated into Greek at a king’s request and then the gospel carried there by the evangelist. Wesley says the worship will be spiritual, though signified by typical phrases.

The smiting that heals is where Calvin and Ellicott converge. Ellicott admits the tone seems at first at odds with the sternness the chapter opened with, and answers that the prophet is no eater of his words: he has learnt to look past the chastisement and see that it holds of Egypt as of Israel that whom the Lord loves he chastens, the sword smiting only to heal. Calvin rejects a softer rendering—that God will strike with a wound that may be healed—as weakening the sense, since the wounds themselves are the means of bringing the nation back. Exemption from punishment, he says, would only cherish a freer disposition to sin, and Egypt, which went beyond all nations in idolatry, is the instance of mercy working so; conversion, he adds, may be called a resurrection from eternal death, not that repentance deserves the favour but that God raises us by it out of death into life. Keil and Delitzsch take a longer view and find at least a magnificent prelude to the fulfilment in the state of Egypt before it fell to Islam in the seventh century, grown from that small beginning of five cities, one altar and a single obelisk. Gill and Wesley put it simply: God afflicts them by one providence or another till they are awakened, and by those afflictions converts and saves them.
23:
The highway between the old enemies is read as the widening of the whole prophecy. Charles Ellicott says the prophet’s horizon brightens and expands: the land was in his time the battlefield the two great empires crossed on their marches, and he looks forward to that discord ceasing and both joined with Israel in a threefold cord not easily broken. Like other bright ideals, Ellicott adds, it still waits for fulfilment; the nearest approach is perhaps the Persian monarchy, which held all three territories and acknowledged, in its founder’s proclamations, the Lord as the God of heaven. Adam Clarke points to the same period, when the three countries lived peaceably under one government with regular and uninterrupted intercourse. John Gill allows a show of accomplishment under an Egyptian king but refers it chiefly to the gospel, and John Wesley to enemies reconciled in the service of God. John Calvin takes the two nations as chosen deliberately for their hostility—more might have been expected of distant peoples, since these openly made war on God—so that if he is gracious to the Church’s deadliest enemies the calling of all nations is included. On the last clause he refuses to choose: the words may mean that the two will serve God, or, since the divine name is not expressed, that those who once burned to injure one another will now desire to do each other kindness; he sets out both and leaves every reader to take what he thinks best.

The threefold league is described with care about Israel’s place in it. Keil and Delitzsch call it a tripartite covenant in which Israel forms the third part, and say Israel has now reached the great end of its calling, to be a blessing in the whole circuit of the earth, with Egypt and Assyria standing for all the nations—whereas hitherto its position between the two had been nothing but a disadvantage, as the history of both its kingdoms proves. Gill suggests Israel is third in the sense of mediator, the middle wall of partition being broken down. Wesley makes the pre-eminence explicit, that Israel is not only a third party but the most eminent of the three, the fountain by which the blessing is conveyed to the other two. Calvin observes what the promise costs the older privilege: the grace of God had been confined to one nation, and now he who had adopted none but the children of Abraham wishes to be called the father of all. He also settles a grammatical point, that the word for blessing takes the feminine adjective and means a form or pattern of blessing.

The three titles at the close are weighed one by one. Ellicott notes Israel keeps the spiritual supremacy even here: Egypt, once alien, becomes the people of the Lord, Assyria is recognised as the instrument made to do his work, and Israel has the pre-eminence of being his inheritance. Calvin distinguishes them at more length and to the same effect. To call the Egyptians the people of God means they will share the honour once bestowed peculiarly on the Jews; to call the Assyrians the work of his hands is to give them the title proper to the Church, since believers are made new by the spirit of regeneration to bear God’s image—we are the work of his hands not as men created but as men created again to another life; and Israel keeps the prerogative of the first-born among the new brethren, since the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. Gill extends the blessing to the chosen among Jews and Gentiles alike, and Wesley notes the three are spoken of as one people because united into one church. Clarke closes on unfinished business: all these countries are to be converted, and this, he says, remains partly to be fulfilled—though perhaps at no very distant time.
